text: Stomach Pain and Digestive Emergencies Near White Rock: Appendicitis, Food Poisoning, and Severe Abdominal Pain Care ER of White Rock Stomach and Digestive Medically reviewed by the ER of White Rock Nursing Team |Updated: August 19, 2026 Table of Contents TL;DR: Stomach pain is the most common reason adults visit an emergency room. Most of it is mild and self-limited. A small subset is a surgical or medical emergency where every hour matters: appendicitis, bowel obstruction, perforated ulcer, pancreatitis, severe dehydration, gastrointestinal bleeding. This guide walks through the red flags that separate “wait it out” from “come in now,” the decision points for appendicitis, food poisoning, dehydration, and severe abdominal pain, and how to choose between 911, a freestanding ER, and urgent care near White Rock Lake.Stomach pain hides what it actually is. A dull ache around the navel that drifts to the right lower quadrant can be the early hours of appendicitis. Cramping with watery diarrhea after a buffet meal is usually viral gastroenteritis but can be life-threatening dehydration in a toddler or an older adult. Vomiting blood, passing black stool, or pain so severe you cannot stand up straight is never something to “sleep off.”This guide is written for the moment you or someone in your household is doubled over in pain and trying to decide what to do next. We cover the categories of digestive emergencies we treat every shift, the warning signs that should send you in fast, and the scenarios that need 911 or a hospital surgical team instead of a freestanding ER.ER of White Rock is an independent freestanding emergency room at 10705 Northwest Highway, open 24 hours. We have on-site CT, ultrasound, X-ray, and a full lab, experienced emergency physicians, and direct transfer relationships with general surgery, gastroenterology, and ICU services across the area.How Digestive Emergencies Differ in the ERMost stomach pain belongs at home with rest, fluids, and a clear-liquid diet. The exceptions are the cases where the pain pattern, severity, or accompanying signs point to a surgical abdomen, severe dehydration, or active bleeding.Three questions sort them quickly:Is the pain so severe it stops you from walking, standing straight, or moving in bed?Are there warning signs of bleeding, severe dehydration, or peritonitis: blood in vomit or stool, black stool, rigid abdomen, fever above 103, dizziness on standing, no urine for 8+ hours?Is the pain localized in the right lower quadrant, the upper right, the upper middle, or the back, in a pattern that has been getting worse for more than four hours?A “yes” to severity plus any localized pattern usually means come in for imaging. A “yes” to any bleeding or peritonitis sign means 911 or come in immediately. Mild diffuse cramping with watery diarrhea and no red flags is usually safe to manage at home.The NIDDK overview of digestive diseases emphasizes that abdominal pain with persistent vomiting, fever, or bleeding deserves prompt medical evaluation, and that delayed care for surgical emergencies like appendicitis or bowel obstruction sharply increases complications. For the broader question of which ER to choose, our guide to choosing the right emergency room walks through the decision tree.Appendicitis: The Classic Surgical EmergencyAppendicitis is inflammation of the appendix, a small finger-shaped pouch attached to the start of the large intestine. Untreated, the inflamed appendix can rupture within 24 to 72 hours of symptom onset, spilling bacteria into the abdomen and causing peritonitis. The diagnosis is time-sensitive, and the treatment is surgery.The Classic Pain PatternThe textbook pattern starts with vague pain around the belly button. Over the next 6 to 24 hours, the pain migrates to the right lower quadrant and becomes sharp and constant. Walking, coughing, or pressing on that spot makes the pain worse. Nausea, loss of appetite, and a low-grade fever often follow.Not every case follows the textbook. Children, pregnant patients, and older adults often present atypically. The MedlinePlus appendicitis overview stresses that anyone with persistent right lower quadrant pain plus nausea, fever, or loss of appetite should be evaluated, even if the pattern is not classic.Red Flags to Come in NowRight lower quadrant pain that has been getting worse for more than four hoursPain that is sharp, constant, and worse with walking or coughingLoss of appetite, nausea, vomiting following abdominal painFever above 100.5 with abdominal painSudden relief of pain followed by worse pain with rigid abdomen (possible rupture)Children pulling their knees to their chest, refusing to walk, refusing foodOur on-site appendicitis evaluation includes CT or ultrasound within 30 minutes of arrival, lab workup for infection markers, surgical consultation by phone, and direct transfer to a hospital with general surgery when appendectomy is needed. Most patients are imaged, diagnosed, and en route to the operating facility within two hours of arrival.Severe Abdominal Pain: Beyond AppendicitisSevere abdominal pain has many causes. The job of the ER is to rule out the dangerous ones fast.Patterns That Suggest a Surgical or Dangerous CauseUpper right pain radiating to the right shoulder or back, with nausea after fatty meals: gallbladder attack or gallstonesUpper middle pain boring through to the back, with nausea and vomiting: pancreatitisSharp, sudden, severe pain in the upper abdomen with a rigid board-like belly: perforated ulcerCrampy waves of pain with vomiting, distended belly, no bowel movements or gas: bowel obstructionTearing pain radiating to the back in someone over 60, especially with a known aneurysm: abdominal aortic dissection or rupture (call 911)Right or left lower pain in a pregnant patient: ectopic pregnancy until proven otherwiseThe MedlinePlus overview of abdominal pain notes that pain severe enough to wake you from sleep, pain with a rigid abdomen, or pain with significant vomiting blood or fever needs same-day evaluation, not a “wait and see” approach. Our abdominal pain evaluation covers the full ER workup: physical exam, vital signs, labs, ultrasound, and CT when indicated.The First Hour at HomeWhile arranging transport, do not eat or drink anything (you may need surgery, and an empty stomach is safer). Do not take painkillers that thin the blood (aspirin, ibuprofen). Acetaminophen is generally safe. Do not apply heat to a possibly inflamed appendix or gallbladder. Lie still in whatever position relieves the pain.Food Poisoning vs Stomach Bug: When Either One Becomes an EmergencyMost cases of food poisoning and viral gastroenteritis resolve at home in 24 to 72 hours with rest and fluids. A subset becomes an emergency because of severe dehydration, persistent high fever, blood in stool, or signs that the cause is more dangerous (E. coli, Salmonella, C. difficile, Listeria).Patterns That Suggest a Worse CauseBloody diarrhea (suggests Shigella, E. coli O157, or invasive infection)Fever above 102 that lasts more than 48 hoursSevere abdominal pain that does not improve between vomiting or diarrhea episodesSigns of dehydration: dizziness on standing, no urine for 8+ hours, dry mouth, sunken eyesSymptoms in pregnancy, in an infant, in someone over 65, or in someone with a weakened immune systemSymptoms after eating from a known outbreak source (deli meats, raw oysters, leafy greens)Neurological symptoms with food poisoning (botulism is rare but a 911 call)The CDC food safety overview notes that severe food poisoning cases are most dangerous in the same groups where dehydration is fastest: pregnant patients, infants, older adults, and the immunocompromised. Our food poisoning treatment covers IV fluids, anti-emetics, stool testing when indicated, and direct admission if severe.For the longer comparison between food poisoning and a stomach bug, our deeper guide on recognizing severe food poisoning walks through the cause-by-cause symptom patterns.Dehydration: When Lost Fluids Become a Medical EmergencyDehydration is the most common reason people end up in the ER for a stomach bug. It is also one of the easiest emergencies to miss in toddlers, older adults, and patients with diabetes or kidney disease, because the warning signs are quiet until they are not.Adult Warning SignsNo urine in the past 8 hours, or urine that is dark like apple juiceDizziness or feeling like you might faint when you stand upRapid heart rate at restDry mouth, no saliva, no tearsConfusion, weakness, or trouble staying awakeInability to keep down even sips of fluid for more than 12 hoursPediatric Warning SignsNo wet diaper in 6 hours (infant) or no urine in 8 hours (child)Crying without tearsSunken eyes or sunken soft spot on a baby’s headLethargy, refusing to play, refusing to drinkSkin that stays “tented” when pinched gently on the back of the handThe MedlinePlus dehydration overview emphasizes that severe dehydration in children can progress to shock in hours, and that ORS (oral rehydration solution) is the preferred home rehydration when the child can keep sips down. Our dehydration treatment includes IV fluid resuscitation, electrolyte correction, anti-emetics so the child can resume oral fluids, and observation until safe to discharge.Gastrointestinal Bleeding: Always an EmergencyGI bleeding can come from the upper tract (esophagus, stomach, duodenum) or the lower tract (colon, rectum). The patient may not know they are bleeding internally until they pass black tarry stool, vomit something that looks like coffee grounds, or feel suddenly weak and pale.Red FlagsVomiting bright red blood or material that looks like coffee groundsPassing black, tarry stools (melena) or maroon stoolsBright red blood in stool that is more than a few drops or that recursSudden severe weakness, dizziness, or lightheadednessPale skin, cold sweats, rapid heart rateHistory of ulcers, liver disease, or blood thinnersAny of these patterns means come in immediately. Severe upper GI bleeding can drop blood pressure within an hour and is a transfusion-and-endoscopy emergency. Our gastrointestinal disease evaluation includes type-and-screen, IV access for transfusion, gastric tube placement when needed, and direct transfer to a hospital with on-call gastroenterology and endoscopy when the bleeding is significant.Real-World Scenarios Near White Rock LakeThe categories above are the framework. The moment of decision happens in messy specifics. Here are five scenarios that play out near White Rock Lake every week.Teenager with Right Lower Pain in Lake HighlandsA 14-year-old has been complaining of belly pain since breakfast. It started around the belly button. By dinner it has moved to the right lower side. They refuse food, they want to lie still, and they have a low fever.This is appendicitis until proven otherwise. Come in. We can run labs, do an ultrasound or CT within 30 minutes, and have a surgical consult on the line before imaging is complete. Most pediatric appendicitis cases are at our ER, diagnosed, and en route to a pediatric surgical hospital within two hours.Toddler with Vomiting and No Wet DiaperA two-year-old has been vomiting for 18 hours. They had a brief watery diarrhea, refused fluids for the past four hours, and have had no wet diaper since this morning. They are quieter than usual and harder to console.This is moderate to severe pediatric dehydration. Come in. We can start a small IV, give an anti-nausea med, run electrolytes, and have the child taking sips within an hour. Most pediatric dehydration cases discharge home the same visit once tolerating oral fluids.Adult with Sudden Severe Upper Abdominal PainA 55-year-old with a history of ulcers wakes up at 2 a.m. with severe upper abdominal pain. They cannot get comfortable. Their belly feels rigid when they press on it.This is a possible perforated ulcer. Call 911 or come in immediately. An upright chest X-ray to look for free air under the diaphragm, IV access, and surgical consult are the first steps. Perforation is a true surgical emergency.Family Sick After a Restaurant MealFour members of a family develop vomiting and watery diarrhea within hours of eating the same restaurant meal. One child cannot keep down any fluids. The adults are tolerating sips but feel weak.The child needs to come in for fluid resuscitation and possible stool testing. The adults can usually manage at home with ORS, but should come in if they develop fever above 102, bloody stool, or signs of dehydration. Our deeper food poisoning guide covers the cause-by-cause pattern.Older Adult Passing Black StoolA 70-year-old on blood thinners passes black tarry stool twice in one day. They feel weak and dizzy when they stand up.This is upper GI bleeding until proven otherwise. Call us before driving, or have someone drive. We will type-and-screen blood, start IV fluids, and arrange direct transfer to a hospital with endoscopy on call. Time matters more than distance for this presentation.How a Freestanding ER Handles Digestive EmergenciesA freestanding ER in Texas is licensed and equipped to evaluate and stabilize the full range of abdominal emergencies, with the exception of cases that need an operating room or ICU on site. For most digestive presentations, the workflow looks like this:Triage at the door, with immediate vitals, IV access, and a focused abdominal examLabs (CBC, chem, lipase, liver panel, type and screen) drawn and run in our on-site lab within 30 minutesUltrasound for suspected gallstones or ectopic pregnancyCT for suspected appendicitis, bowel obstruction, pancreatitis, perforation, or unexplained severe abdominal painPain control, anti-emetics, IV fluids, and broad-spectrum antibiotics when indicatedSurgical or GI consultation by phone with hospital specialistsDirect transfer to a hospital with the right specialty service when surgery, ICU, or endoscopy is neededThe fastest path to definitive care for a surgical abdomen depends on the diagnosis, not on the size of the building. For a single-system presentation, a freestanding ER is often the quickest route to answers, because the scan is ordered, taken, and read on site. Our on-site CT and ultrasound typically images patients within 20 minutes of the order, and our on-site lab turns around CBC, chemistry, and lipase results in under 30 minutes.How to Decide in the MomentWhen the moment hits, the framework should be simple.Call 911 if: the person has a rigid board-like abdomen, is vomiting bright red blood, is passing large amounts of blood from the rectum, has tearing pain radiating to the back (possible aneurysm), is too weak to walk, has chest pain with the abdominal pain, or has a known aneurysm history.Go to a freestanding ER if: the pain is severe and localized, the patient is alert, and there is no major bleeding or cardiovascular instability. Suspected appendicitis. Gallbladder attack. Pancreatitis. Severe vomiting and dehydration. Suspected food poisoning with high fever or blood in stool. Toddler dehydration. Adult abdominal pain that has been worsening for more than four hours.Go straight to a surgical center if: the case is a confirmed surgical emergency the team has told you to come straight to, or there is major polytrauma alongside the abdominal complaint.Do not go to urgent care if: the pain is severe, localized, and worsening; if there is blood in vomit or stool; if dehydration is significant; or if the patient is pregnant, elderly, immunocompromised, or younger than 2. Urgent care clinics do not have CT or in-house surgery consultation. The time you lose backtracking is time you cannot get back.For the broader decision framework, our guide to choosing the right emergency room covers the full picture.Pediatric Stomach PainChildren are not small adults. Their dehydration is faster, their appendicitis is harder to diagnose, and they cannot always describe where the pain is. A child who is quieter than usual, who refuses food, who pulls knees to chest, or who cannot be consoled deserves evaluation even before the textbook pattern shows up.For pediatric stomach pain, a freestanding ER is often a strong first stop because of the speed and the quieter environment. We have pediatric-sized equipment, weight-based dosing, and clear protocols for when a child needs Children’s Medical Center Dallas or another pediatric specialty hospital instead. Our parent’s guide to pediatric emergency care near White Rock covers the full set of pediatric red flags.Frequently Asked QuestionsHow do I know if my stomach pain is appendicitis or just a stomach bug?The two often look similar in the first hours. Patterns that point toward appendicitis: pain that starts around the navel and migrates to the right lower side, pain that is constant and worse with walking or coughing, loss of appetite, and a low-grade fever. Patterns that point toward a stomach bug: diffuse cramping that comes in waves, vomiting and diarrhea, and pain that improves between episodes. If the pain has been getting worse over four to six hours and is localized to the right lower quadrant, come in for imaging.When does food poisoning need an ER visit?Most cases recover at home in 24 to 72 hours. Come in if you have bloody diarrhea, fever above 102 for more than 48 hours, severe abdominal pain between episodes, signs of dehydration (no urine for 8+ hours, dizziness on standing), or if the patient is pregnant, under 2, over 65, or immunocompromised.What is the fastest way to rehydrate at home?Oral rehydration solution (ORS) products like Pedialyte are absorbed faster than plain water because they include the right balance of sodium, potassium, and glucose. Start with small sips every 5 to 10 minutes. Avoid sports drinks and sugary sodas, which can worsen diarrhea. If sips cannot be kept down for more than 12 hours, come in for IV fluids.Is black stool always a GI bleed?Iron supplements, bismuth (Pepto-Bismol), and some foods can darken stool. True melena from upper GI bleeding is sticky, tarry, and has a strong distinctive odor. If you are taking iron or bismuth, mention it. If you are not, treat black stool as a possible bleed and come in.Can a freestanding ER do surgery for appendicitis?No. Freestanding ERs in Texas do not have operating rooms. We diagnose the appendicitis fast with on-site CT or ultrasound, stabilize with IV fluids and antibiotics, and transfer directly to a hospital with general surgery. The transfer moves quickly because the workup is already done and travels with the patient.What should I do for severe stomach pain while waiting to be seen?Do not eat or drink anything (NPO) in case surgery is needed. Do not take aspirin or ibuprofen, which can worsen bleeding and irritate the stomach. Acetaminophen for fever is generally safe. Do not apply heat to the abdomen. Lie in whatever position is most comfortable.Will my insurance cover an ER visit for stomach pain?Yes. ER visits are covered under your plan’s emergency room cost-sharing tier regardless of which ER you visit. Texas SB 1264 plus the federal No Surprises Act blocks balance billing for most emergency services.How fast can I get imaging at a freestanding ER?On-site CT and ultrasound typically image patients within 20 minutes of the order. Radiologist reads come back through 24/7 teleradiology, often within the next 30 minutes.Where We Are and How to Reach UsER of White Rock is at 10705 Northwest Highway, Dallas, TX 75238, minutes from White Rock Lake, Lakewood, Lake Highlands, Casa View, Casa Linda, and Forest Hills. We are open 24 hours a day, every day, including holidays.If the pain is severe, the abdomen feels rigid, or you suspect a major GI bleed, call 911 first. If the case is concerning but the patient is stable, call us at (469) 943-2939 and an ER nurse can help triage by phone. For directions and hours, visit our contact page.Knowing the red flags before you need them is the best preparation. Save this page. Save our number. And teach the warning signs of appendicitis and dehydration to anyone in your household with kids or older parents.Latest Insights: What to Tell the ER Team: A Medication and Symptom Note Read More ... text: Emergencias de Huesos, Articulaciones y Trauma cerca de White Rock: Fracturas, Lesiones de Cabeza y Cuidado de Lesiones Oculares Admin mayo 12, 2026 Trauma and Injury Tabla de Contenido Resumen: Las emergencias de huesos, articulaciones y trauma dependen de tres cosas: la energía del impacto, la parte del cuerpo afectada y las señales de alarma que aparecen después. Una fractura simple de muñeca no es la misma llamada que una lesión de cabeza con vómito, y una salpicadura química en el ojo no es la misma llamada que un tobillo torcido. Esta guía explica cómo reconocer las banderas rojas de fracturas, lesiones de cabeza, conmociones cerebrales, lesión cerebral traumática (TBI), lesiones oculares y dolor de espalda, qué hacer en la primera hora y cómo elegir entre llamar al 911, una sala de emergencias independiente y una sala hospitalaria cerca de White Rock Lake.Escuchas el chasquido antes de sentir el dolor. O tu hijo se cae de un patín y diez minutos después no recuerda la conversación que acabas de tener. O alguien en el trabajo se salpica un limpiador en el ojo y la córnea empieza a arder.El trauma es ruidoso o silencioso. Las fracturas y las caídas dramáticas llaman la atención. Las conmociones cerebrales, los sangrados lentos del cerebro y las lesiones oculares serias pueden esconderse por horas antes de manifestarse.Esta guía está escrita para el momento en que una lesión acaba de ocurrir y la familia está tratando de decidir qué hacer después. Cubrimos las categorías de trauma de hueso, articulación y cabeza que tratamos en cada turno en nuestra sala de emergencias, las señales de alarma que deben llevarte a venir rápido, y los escenarios que necesitan un hospital pediátrico o un centro de trauma Nivel I en su lugar.ER of White Rock es una sala de emergencias independiente en 10705 Northwest Highway, abierta las 24 horas. Tenemos rayos X, tomografía computarizada (CT) y ultrasonido en el sitio, médicos de emergencia con experiencia, y relaciones directas de transferencia con especialistas en ortopedia, neurocirugía y oftalmología en el área.Cómo se Diferencian las Lesiones de Huesos, Articulaciones y Trauma en la Sala de EmergenciasLa mayor parte del trauma se puede tratar en una sala de emergencias independiente. Las excepciones son los casos que necesitan cirugía especializada, cuidado intensivo o un equipo de trauma de nivel uno en la primera hora.Tres preguntas las clasifican rápido:¿Fue la energía de la lesión lo bastante alta para amenazar más de una parte del cuerpo? (Choque de auto, caída desde altura, motocicleta.)¿Hay una deformidad obvia, una herida abierta que expone el hueso, o una extremidad que no se puede mover en absoluto?¿Hay señales de alarma de lesión interna: confusión, dolor abdominal severo, pérdida súbita de visión, debilidad en un lado, caída de los rasgos faciales?Un «sí» a cualquiera de esas significa 911 y un centro de trauma hospitalario, no una sala independiente. Un «no» usualmente significa que una sala independiente es el camino más rápido a las imágenes y al tratamiento.La visión general de prevención de lesiones de los CDC recuerda a las familias que la mayoría de las lesiones no intencionales ocurren en casa, en la carretera o durante la recreación, y que la evaluación temprana cambia los resultados para lesiones de cabeza y fracturas en particular. Para la pregunta más amplia de cuál sala de emergencias elegir, nuestra guía sobre sala independiente vs hospitalaria recorre el árbol de decisión.Fracturas y Huesos Posiblemente RotosUna fractura es cualquier ruptura del hueso. La ruptura puede ser una fisura tan fina que apenas se ve en una radiografía, o puede ser una fractura abierta con hueso visible a través de la piel. Ambas necesitan imágenes y evaluación clínica. Solo una necesita cirugía.Señales que Sugieren Fuertemente una FracturaEl patrón clásico después de una caída, una torsión o un golpe directo incluye:Dolor que no mejora con reposo, hielo y elevación durante la primera horaHinchazón y moretones que crecen rápido alrededor del sitio de la lesiónDeformidad visible o una extremidad que se ve torcidaIncapacidad para apoyar peso en una pierna o usar un brazo normalmenteAdormecimiento, hormigueo, o piel pálida o fría debajo de la lesiónHueso visible a través de la piel rota (fractura abierta, siempre una llamada al 911)La página de MedlinePlus sobre fracturas señala que cualquier fractura con deformidad significativa, herida abierta o pérdida de pulso debajo de la lesión es una verdadera emergencia. Las fracturas más pequeñas de dedos, pies, costillas o huesos que no soportan peso usualmente pueden esperar el tiempo que toma manejar a una sala de emergencias independiente, pero deben evaluarse el mismo día.La Primera HoraInmoviliza la lesión exactamente como la encuentras. No trates de enderezar una extremidad deformada. Aplica una férula con lo que tengas a mano (una revista enrollada, una tabla, una toalla doblada) y acolchónala bien. Eleva la extremidad por encima del corazón si es posible. Aplica hielo a través de una tela, nunca directo sobre la piel.Después ven. Nuestra evaluación de fracturas en el sitio incluye radiografía a los pocos minutos de la llegada, ferulización o reducción en la sala de emergencias para fracturas simples, y referencia directa a un cirujano ortopédico cuando una fractura necesita hardware o una reparación especializada. Nuestra suite de CT y rayos X en el sitio usualmente toma imágenes dentro de 20 minutos de la orden.Lesión de Cabeza y Conmoción CerebralEl cerebro es el órgano más implacable en el trauma. Un golpe que parece menor en el momento puede esconder un sangrado lento que se vuelve serio seis a doce horas después, que es la razón por la que cada lesión de cabeza con banderas rojas pertenece en la sala de emergencias para evaluación.Las Banderas Rojas de HEADS UPEl programa HEADS UP de los CDC enumera las señales de alarma que convierten una lesión de cabeza de «observar en casa» a «ir a la sala de emergencias ahora»:Pérdida del conocimiento, aunque sea breveVómito más de una vez después de la lesiónUn dolor de cabeza severo o que empeoraHabla arrastrada, debilidad, adormecimiento o convulsiónConfusión, agitación o conducta inusualDificultad para despertarse, o sueño más profundo de lo normalLíquido claro o sangre que drena de la nariz o de los oídosPupilas de tamaño desigualCualquiera de estas señales en una persona que se golpeó la cabeza significa que el estudio debe incluir una tomografía computarizada de cabeza sin contraste. Nuestra evaluación de lesión de cabeza de emergencia puede completar el CT en minutos y tener la lectura del radiólogo de regreso rápido.Conmoción Cerebral: TBI LeveUna conmoción cerebral es una lesión cerebral traumática leve causada por un golpe o sacudida a la cabeza que interrumpe la función cerebral por un corto tiempo. Los signos distintivos son confusión, una breve pérdida del conocimiento, dolor de cabeza, mareo, náusea y pensamiento lento. La memoria del evento alrededor del impacto puede faltar.El Instituto Nacional de Trastornos Neurológicos y Accidentes Cerebrovasculares enfatiza que incluso una sola conmoción cerebral merece evaluación clínica, y que volver a los deportes o al trabajo demasiado pronto aumenta el riesgo de una segunda lesión peor. Nuestra ruta de evaluación de conmoción cerebral cubre revisión de síntomas, examen neurológico, guía de regreso al juego y referencia de seguimiento cuando es necesaria.Lesión Cerebral Traumática (TBI): Cuando las Cosas se Ponen SeriasLa TBI va desde el extremo leve (conmoción cerebral) hasta lesiones cerebrales severas con coma prolongado. Los extremos medio y severo requieren evaluación inmediata en la sala de emergencias y a menudo un centro neuroquirúrgico.Señales de alarma de que una lesión de cabeza ha cruzado a TBI moderada o severa:Pérdida del conocimiento que dura más de 30 segundosConfusión persistente o incapacidad para seguir órdenesUna pupila más grande que la otraConvulsiónVómito que no paraDolor de cabeza severo que escalaDebilidad o adormecimiento en un lado del cuerpoPara cualquiera de estas, llama al 911. La instalación receptora correrá un CT en la primera hora, y si hay sangrado significativo el equipo transfiere a un hospital con neurocirugía de guardia. Nuestra evaluación y estabilización de TBI explica el estudio estándar de la sala de emergencias y el modelo de estabilizar-y-transferir para casos severos.Lesiones Oculares: Romas, Cortantes y QuímicasLas lesiones oculares son sensibles al tiempo de una manera que sorprende a la mayoría de las familias. Una salpicadura química daña la córnea en segundos. Una lesión penetrante puede comprometer la visión permanentemente si el estudio se retrasa.Salpicadura Química en el OjoEsta es la única emergencia en la que debes empezar el tratamiento antes de salir de casa. Enjuaga el ojo con agua fría continuamente por al menos 15 a 20 minutos. Después llama al 911 o ven directo. La Academia Americana de Oftalmología enfatiza que la duración del enjuague importa mucho más que la velocidad de llegada a la sala de emergencias, porque el daño químico continúa hasta que la sustancia se lava.Cuerpo Extraño, Abrasión Corneal y Trauma RomoUn cuerpo extraño en el ojo, un rasguño corneal de una uña o una rama de árbol, o un impacto romo de una pelota o un puño todos necesitan evaluación. Vigila:Material extraño visible que el paciente no puede parpadear para sacarDolor severo que no mejora con unos minutos de reposoCambio repentino de visión, visión doble o pérdida parcial de visiónSangre dentro de la parte de color del ojo (hipema)Pupilas que se ven de tamaños diferentes, o una pupila que no se contrae con la luzUn ojo que sobresale o se asienta diferente en la cuencaNuestra evaluación de lesiones oculares cubre examen con lámpara de hendidura, tinción con fluoresceína para abrasiones corneales, remoción de cuerpos extraños, y referencia directa a un oftalmólogo cuando es necesaria.Dolor de Espalda: Cuándo Cruza a una EmergenciaLa mayor parte del dolor de espalda es muscular y se recupera con reposo y fisioterapia. Un grupo pequeño de presentaciones cruza a territorio emergente porque sugieren compromiso de la médula espinal o de un nervio mayor.Señales de alarma de dolor de espalda:Adormecimiento nuevo en la ingle, el perineo o la cara interna superior de los muslos («anestesia en silla de montar»)Pérdida nueva del control de intestinos o vejigaDebilidad progresiva en una o ambas piernasFiebre acompañada de dolor de espalda, especialmente en alguien con historia de drogas intravenosas o infección recienteDolor de espalda severo después de una caída, choque de auto u otro impacto significativoDolor de espalda con pérdida de peso, dolor nocturno o historia conocida de cáncerLa página de MedlinePlus sobre dolor de espalda cubre cuándo el autocuidado es suficiente y cuándo se requiere evaluación. La anestesia en silla de montar más la disfunción nueva de intestinos o vejiga es síndrome de cola de caballo, una verdadera emergencia neuroquirúrgica donde cada hora de retraso arriesga daño permanente. Llama al 911 para ese patrón.Esguinces vs Fracturas: Por Qué Importa la DiferenciaEn casa, un esguince y una fractura pueden verse idénticos: hinchazón, dolor, moretones, dificultad para usar la extremidad. La diferencia a menudo es invisible hasta que tienes una radiografía.Las reglas de Ottawa, desarrolladas por médicos de emergencia y usadas mundialmente, son una herramienta de decisión clínica que ayuda a determinar cuáles lesiones de tobillo o rodilla en realidad necesitan una radiografía. Los patrones que casi siempre justifican imágenes incluyen:Incapacidad para apoyar peso por cuatro pasos inmediatamente después de la lesiónSensibilidad ósea directamente sobre el borde posterior de cualquier maléolo (los huesos del tobillo)Sensibilidad ósea sobre el navicular o el quinto metatarsiano del pieIncapacidad para flexionar la rodilla a 90 gradosSensibilidad ósea sobre la rótula o la cabeza del peronéSi alguno de estos aplica, ven para imágenes. Una fractura no detectada y tratada como esguince puede sanar en una posición deformada y crear un problema articular de por vida.Escenarios del Mundo Real cerca de White Rock LakeLas categorías de arriba son el marco. El momento de decisión ocurre en detalles desordenados. Aquí cinco escenarios que ocurren cerca de White Rock Lake cada semana.Caída de Trampolín en Lake HighlandsUn niño aterriza torpemente al bajar de un trampolín del patio y ahora favorece un brazo. La muñeca se ve ligeramente doblada pero la piel está intacta. No hay lesión de cabeza, no hay pérdida del conocimiento, no hay vómito.Esta es una llamada típica para una sala de emergencias independiente. Trae al niño. Podemos ferulizar, tomar radiografía, reducir una fractura simple y arreglar el seguimiento ortopédico en la misma visita. La mayoría de las fracturas pediátricas de antebrazo se tratan en la sala de emergencias y nunca necesitan admisión hospitalaria.Colisión Deportiva con Breve Pérdida de MemoriaUn atleta de secundaria recibe un golpe fuerte durante un partido, camina fuera y no puede recordar la jugada. El dolor de cabeza empieza cinco minutos después. No hay vómito, no hay debilidad, no hay convulsión.Esto es una conmoción cerebral hasta que se demuestre lo contrario. Ven para evaluación. Completamos un examen neurológico, decidimos sobre imágenes basados en los criterios HEADS UP y proveemos guía de regreso al juego basada en protocolos actuales de conmoción. La mayoría de los pacientes se van a casa el mismo día con instrucciones de reposo y disparadores claros de escalada.Salpicadura Química en el TrabajoUn empleado se salpica un desengrasante en el ojo en el trabajo. El ojo arde y lagrimea de inmediato.Empieza a enjuagar en el lugar, en la estación de lavado de ojos del trabajo si está disponible, por al menos 15 a 20 minutos. Después ven directo a la sala de emergencias. Continuamos la irrigación al llegar, revisamos el pH, corremos un examen con fluoresceína y conectamos con un oftalmólogo si la córnea está significativamente dañada.Caída Mayor desde AlturaAlguien se cae de un techo, de una escalera alta o por unas escaleras y no puede mover una extremidad, o tiene dolor de cuello, o estuvo brevemente inconsciente.Llama al 911. Los paramédicos pondrán al paciente en tabla y collar y lo enrutarán directo a un centro de trauma Nivel I o II. Este es el caso donde saltarse una sala independiente por un centro de trauma designado ahorra más tiempo.Adormecimiento Súbito en Silla de Montar con Dolor de EspaldaUn adulto desarrolla dolor de espalda que empeora, después nota adormecimiento en la cara interna de los muslos y dificultad para empezar a orinar.Esto es síndrome de cola de caballo hasta que se demuestre lo contrario. Llama al 911. El estudio en el hospital receptor es MRI urgente de la columna lumbar y consulta de neurocirugía. El tiempo hasta la descompresión es el factor más grande para que la función se recupere.Cómo una Sala de Emergencias Independiente Maneja los Casos de TraumaUna sala de emergencias independiente en Texas está licenciada y equipada para evaluar y estabilizar todo el rango de trauma, con la excepción de politraumatismos mayores que necesitan un quirófano o UCI en el sitio. Para huesos, articulaciones y la mayoría de las lesiones de cabeza y ojos, el flujo de trabajo se ve así:Triaje en la puerta, con signos vitales inmediatos y un examen de trauma enfocadoRayos X, CT o ultrasonido a los pocos minutos de la orden, leído por un servicio de teleradiología 24/7Control del dolor, acceso IV y actualización de tétanos cuando es apropiadoFerulización, reducción simple, sutura o irrigación ocular hechas en la salaConsulta con especialistas por teléfono con ortopedia, neurocirugía u oftalmología cuando se necesitaTransferencia directa a un centro de trauma hospitalario o servicio especializado cuando la lesión excede lo que puede arreglar una sala independienteEl camino más rápido al cuidado definitivo de trauma rara vez es «manejar al hospital más grande.» Para lesiones de un solo sistema, una sala independiente suele ser la ruta más rápida a un diagnóstico, porque el estudio se ordena, se toma y se lee en el sitio. Para politraumatismos mayores, un centro de trauma designado es el destino correcto desde el principio.Para contexto de laboratorio e imágenes, nuestro laboratorio en el sitio entrega resultados de CBC, química y coagulación en menos de 30 minutos cuando el estudio de una fractura o lesión de cabeza los necesita.Cómo Decidir en el MomentoCuando llega el momento, el marco debe ser simple.Llama al 911 si: la persona está inconsciente, tiene una convulsión, sangra abundantemente, tiene una posible lesión espinal, tiene señales de trauma severo de cabeza (una pupila más grande que la otra, vómito repetido, debilidad en un lado), tiene exposición química en la cara o los ojos con dolor severo, o se ha caído desde altura.Ven a una sala de emergencias independiente si: la lesión es de un solo sistema y el paciente está alerta y estable. Sospecha de fractura sin deformidad. Lesión de cabeza leve a moderada con banderas rojas HEADS UP. Cuerpo extraño en el ojo o abrasión corneal simple. Esguince que necesita imágenes. Evaluación de conmoción cerebral.Ve a un centro de trauma si: hay politraumatismo mayor, una fractura abierta confirmada con pérdida significativa de sangre, una emergencia quirúrgica conocida, o si tu especialista te dijo que vayas directo a una instalación específica.No vayas a una clínica de cuidado urgente si: la lesión podría ser una fractura, una lesión de cabeza con banderas rojas, o cualquier lesión ocular más allá de un cuerpo extraño diminuto. Las clínicas de cuidado urgente no tienen CT, y muchas no tienen rayos X. El tiempo que pierdes regresando a una sala de emergencias es tiempo que no puedes recuperar.Para el marco de decisión más amplio, nuestra guía sobre sala independiente vs hospitalaria cubre el cuadro completo.Trauma PediátricoLos niños no son adultos pequeños. Sus huesos se doblan antes de romperse, sus cabezas son proporcionalmente más grandes, y una lesión de cabeza que parecería leve en un adulto puede ser más preocupante en un niño pequeño.Para fracturas, lesiones de cabeza y lesiones oculares pediátricas, una sala de emergencias independiente a menudo es un primer destino fuerte por la velocidad y un ambiente más tranquilo. Tenemos equipo del tamaño pediátrico, dosis basadas en peso y protocolos claros para cuándo un niño necesita Children’s Medical Center Dallas u otro hospital pediátrico especializado.Nuestra guía para padres sobre cuidado de emergencia pediátrico cerca de White Rock cubre el conjunto completo de banderas rojas pediátricas. El trauma pediátrico mayor, sospecha de abuso infantil, lesiones de cabeza con signos neurológicos y lesiones ortopédicas complejas que pueden necesitar cirugía ortopédica pediátrica se estabilizan con nosotros y se transfieren rápido.Preguntas Frecuentes¿Cómo sé si es un esguince o una fractura sin una radiografía?Usualmente no puedes. Las reglas de Ottawa dan pistas clínicas: incapacidad para apoyar peso, sensibilidad ósea sobre puntos específicos, pero la única manera de estar seguro es una radiografía. Si el dolor es severo, la hinchazón es rápida, la extremidad se ve deformada o no se puede apoyar peso, trátalo como una fractura hasta que las imágenes prueben lo contrario.¿Puedo apoyar peso en un pie o tobillo posiblemente roto?Si no puedes dar cuatro pasos justo después de la lesión, la probabilidad de una fractura es lo bastante alta para justificar una radiografía. Incluso si puedes, el dolor persistente sobre un hueso (no solo en el tejido blando) merece evaluación.¿Cuándo necesita una lesión de cabeza una tomografía computarizada?Cualquier lesión de cabeza con pérdida del conocimiento, vómito más de una vez, dolor de cabeza severo o que empeora, confusión, habla arrastrada, convulsión, debilidad o drenaje de la nariz o los oídos necesita un CT. Adultos mayores, personas que toman anticoagulantes y niños muy pequeños también tienen un umbral más bajo.¿Qué debo hacer por una salpicadura ocular antes de llegar a la sala de emergencias?Empieza a enjuagar de inmediato con agua fría por al menos 15 a 20 minutos. No retrases el enjuague para manejar. La duración de la irrigación importa más que la velocidad de la llegada.¿Puede una sala de emergencias independiente componer un hueso roto?Sí. Hacemos reducciones simples, ferulización y enyesado en la sala. Las fracturas complejas que necesitan fijación quirúrgica se estabilizan y se refieren a un cirujano ortopédico, a menudo el mismo día.¿Qué pasa si mi hijo se cayó pero parece estar bien?Vigila las banderas rojas de HEADS UP en las próximas 24 a 48 horas. Cualquier vómito, somnolencia, cambio de comportamiento, problema de equilibrio o dolor de cabeza repetido merece una visita a la sala de emergencias. Las lesiones de cabeza más peligrosas pueden esconderse por horas antes de manifestarse.¿Cubrirá mi seguro una visita a la sala de emergencias por una lesión?Sí. Las visitas a la sala de emergencias están cubiertas bajo el nivel de costos compartidos de tu plan para sala de emergencias sin importar a cuál sala vayas. La ley Texas SB 1264 más la ley federal No Surprises Act bloquean la facturación de saldo para la mayoría de los servicios de emergencia.¿Qué tan rápido puedo obtener imágenes en una sala de emergencias independiente?Los rayos X y CT en el sitio usualmente toman imágenes dentro de 20 minutos de la orden. Las lecturas del radiólogo regresan vía teleradiología 24/7, a menudo dentro de los siguientes 30 minutos. Los resultados se comparten con usted y con el equipo que reciba al paciente si se necesita un traslado.Dónde Estamos y Cómo Llegar a NosotrosER of White Rock está en 10705 Northwest Highway, Dallas, TX 75238, a minutos de White Rock Lake, Lakewood, Lake Highlands, Casa View, Casa Linda y Forest Hills. Estamos abiertos las 24 horas del día, todos los días, incluidos los festivos.Si la lesión es severa o sospechas trauma espinal o mayor de cabeza, llama al 911 primero. Si la lesión es preocupante pero el paciente está estable, llámanos al (469) 943-2939 y una enfermera de emergencias puede ayudar con el triaje por teléfono. Para direcciones y horarios, visita nuestra página de contacto.Conocer las banderas rojas antes de necesitarlas es la mejor preparación. Guarda esta página. Guarda nuestro número. Y enseña las señales de HEADS UP a cualquier persona en tu hogar que tenga niños o juegue deportes de contacto.Últimas Publicaciones: ¿Cuánto Dura una Visita a la Sala de Emergencias? text: Bone, Joint, and Trauma Emergencies Near White Rock: Fractures, Head Injuries, and Eye Injury Care ER of White Rock Trauma and Injury Medically reviewed by the ER of White Rock Nursing Team |Updated: August 19, 2026 Table of Contents TL;DR: Bone, joint, and trauma emergencies turn on three things: the energy of the impact, the body part involved, and the warning signs that follow. A simple wrist fracture is not the same call as a head injury with vomiting, and a chemical splash to the eye is not the same call as a sprained ankle. This guide walks through how to recognize the red flags for fractures, head injuries, concussions, TBI, eye injuries, and back pain, what to do in the first hour, and how to choose between calling 911, a freestanding ER, and a trauma center near White Rock Lake.You hear the snap before you feel the pain. Or your kid falls off a scooter and ten minutes later cannot remember the conversation you just had. Or someone at work splashes a cleaner in their eye and the cornea starts to burn.Trauma is loud or quiet. Bone breaks and dramatic falls grab attention. Concussions, slow brain bleeds, and serious eye injuries can hide for hours before they declare themselves.This guide is written for the moment when an injury just happened and the family is trying to decide what to do next. We cover the categories of bone, joint, and head trauma we treat every shift at our ER, the warning signs that should send you in fast, and the scenarios that need a children’s hospital or a Level I trauma center instead.ER of White Rock is an independent freestanding emergency room at 10705 Northwest Highway, open 24 hours a day. We have on-site X-ray, CT, and ultrasound, experienced emergency physicians, and direct transfer relationships with orthopedic, neurosurgery, and ophthalmology specialists across the area.How Bone, Joint, and Trauma Injuries Differ in the ERMost trauma is treatable at a freestanding ER. The exceptions are the cases that need specialty surgery, intensive care, or a level-one trauma team in the first hour.Three questions sort them quickly:Was the energy of the injury high enough to threaten more than one body part? (Car crash, fall from height, motorcycle.)Is there an obvious deformity, an open wound exposing bone, or a limb that cannot be moved at all?Are there warning signs of internal injury, such as confusion, severe abdominal pain, sudden vision loss, weakness on one side, or drooping facial features?A “yes” to any of those means 911 and a hospital trauma center, not a freestanding ER. A “no” usually means a freestanding ER is the faster path to imaging and treatment.The CDC injury prevention overview reminds families that most unintentional injuries happen at home, on the road, or during recreation, and that early evaluation changes outcomes for head injuries and fractures in particular. For the broader question of which ER to choose, our guide to choosing the right emergency room walks through the decision tree.Fractures and Suspected Broken BonesA fracture is any break in the bone. The break can be a hairline crack you can barely see on an X-ray, or it can be an open fracture with bone visible through the skin. Both need imaging and clinical evaluation. Only one needs surgery.Signs That Strongly Suggest a FractureThe classic pattern after a fall, twist, or direct blow includes:Pain that does not improve with rest, ice, and elevation over the first hourSwelling and bruising that grows quickly around the injury siteVisible deformity or a limb that looks crookedInability to bear weight on a leg or to use an arm normallyNumbness, tingling, or pale or cool skin downstream of the injuryBone visible through broken skin (open fracture, always a 911 call)MedlinePlus fractures overview notes that any fracture with significant deformity, open wound, or loss of pulse downstream is a true emergency. Smaller fractures of fingers, toes, ribs, or non-weight-bearing bones can usually wait the time it takes to drive to a freestanding ER, but they should still be evaluated the same day.The First HourImmobilize the injury exactly as you find it. Do not try to straighten a deformed limb. Apply a splint with whatever is on hand (a rolled magazine, a board, a folded towel) and pad it well. Elevate the limb above the heart if possible. Apply ice through a cloth, never directly to skin.Then come in. Our on-site fracture evaluation includes X-ray within minutes of arrival, splinting or reduction in the ER for simple breaks, and direct referral to an orthopedic surgeon when a fracture needs hardware or a specialty repair. Our on-site CT and X-ray suite typically images patients within 20 minutes of the order.Head Injury and ConcussionThe brain is the most unforgiving organ in trauma. A bump that looks minor at the moment can hide a slow bleed that turns serious six to twelve hours later, which is the reason every head injury with red flags belongs in the ER for evaluation.The HEADS UP Red FlagsThe CDC HEADS UP program lists the warning signs that change a head injury from “watch at home” to “go to the ER now”:Loss of consciousness, even brieflyVomiting more than once after the injuryA severe or worsening headacheSlurred speech, weakness, numbness, or seizureConfusion, agitation, or unusual behaviorTrouble waking up, or sleep that is deeper than normalClear fluid or blood draining from the nose or earsPupils of unequal sizeAny one of these signs in a person who hit their head means the workup should include a non-contrast CT scan of the head. Our emergency head injury evaluation can complete the CT within minutes and have the radiologist read back fast.Concussion, or Mild TBIA concussion is a mild traumatic brain injury caused by a blow or jolt to the head that disrupts brain function for a short time. The hallmarks are confusion, a brief loss of consciousness, headache, dizziness, nausea, and slowed thinking. Memory of the event around the impact may be missing.The National Institute of Neurological Disorders and Stroke emphasizes that even a single concussion deserves clinical evaluation, and that returning to sports or work too soon increases the risk of a worse second injury. Our concussion evaluation pathway covers symptom check, neurologic exam, return-to-play guidance, and follow-up referral when needed.Traumatic Brain Injury (TBI): When Things Get SeriousTBI ranges from the mild end (concussion) to severe brain injuries with prolonged coma. The middle and severe ends require immediate ER evaluation and often a neurosurgical center.Warning signs that a head injury has crossed into moderate or severe TBI:Loss of consciousness lasting more than 30 secondsPersistent confusion or inability to follow commandsOne pupil larger than the otherSeizureVomiting that will not stopSevere, escalating headacheWeakness or numbness on one side of the bodyFor any of these, call 911. The receiving facility will run a CT in the first hour, and if there is significant bleeding the team transfers to a hospital with neurosurgery on call. Our TBI evaluation and stabilization page walks through the standard ER workup and the stabilize-and-transfer model for severe cases.Eye Injuries: Blunt, Sharp, and ChemicalEye injuries are time-sensitive in a way that surprises most families. A chemical splash damages the cornea within seconds. A penetrating injury can compromise vision permanently if the workup is delayed.Chemical Splash to the EyeThis is the one emergency where you should start treatment before you even leave the house. Flush the eye with cool tap water continuously for at least 15 to 20 minutes. Then call 911 or come straight in. The American Academy of Ophthalmology emphasizes that the duration of the rinse matters far more than the speed of arrival at the ER, because the chemical damage continues until the substance is washed out.Foreign Body, Corneal Abrasion, and Blunt TraumaA foreign body in the eye, a corneal scratch from a fingernail or a tree branch, or a blunt impact from a ball or fist all need evaluation. Watch for:Visible foreign material the patient cannot blink outSevere pain that does not improve with a few minutes of restSudden vision change, double vision, or partial vision lossBlood inside the colored part of the eye (hyphema)Pupils that look different sizes, or one pupil that does not constrict to lightAn eye that bulges or sits differently in the socketOur eye injury evaluation covers slit-lamp exam, fluorescein staining for corneal abrasions, foreign body removal, and direct referral to an ophthalmologist when needed.Back Pain: When It Crosses Into an EmergencyMost back pain is muscular and recovers with rest and physical therapy. A small set of presentations cross into emergent territory because they suggest spinal cord or major nerve compromise.Red-flag back pain warning signs:New numbness in the groin, perineum, or upper inner thighs (“saddle anesthesia”)New loss of bowel or bladder controlProgressive weakness in one or both legsFever paired with back pain, especially in someone with IV drug history or recent infectionSevere back pain after a fall, car crash, or other significant impactBack pain with weight loss, night pain, or known cancer historyThe MedlinePlus back pain overview covers when self-care is enough and when evaluation is required. Saddle anesthesia plus new bowel or bladder dysfunction is cauda equina syndrome, a true neurosurgical emergency where every hour of delay risks permanent damage. Call 911 for that pattern.Sprains vs Fractures: Why the Difference MattersAt home, a sprain and a fracture can look identical: swelling, pain, bruising, difficulty using the limb. The difference is often invisible until you have an X-ray.The Ottawa rules, developed by emergency physicians and used worldwide, are a clinical decision tool that helps determine which ankle or knee injuries actually need an X-ray. Patterns that almost always warrant imaging include:Inability to bear weight for four steps immediately after the injuryBone tenderness directly over the back edge of either malleolus (the ankle bones)Bone tenderness over the navicular or fifth metatarsal of the footInability to flex the knee to 90 degreesBone tenderness over the patella or fibular headIf any of these apply, come in for imaging. A missed fracture treated as a sprain can heal in a deformed position and create a lifelong joint problem.Real-World Scenarios Near White Rock LakeThe categories above are the framework. The moment of decision happens in messy specifics. Here are five scenarios that play out near White Rock Lake every week.Trampoline Fall in Lake HighlandsA child lands awkwardly off a backyard trampoline and is now favoring one arm. The wrist looks slightly bent but the skin is intact. There is no head injury, no loss of consciousness, no vomiting.This is a textbook freestanding ER call. Bring the child in. We can splint, X-ray, reduce a simple fracture, and arrange orthopedic follow-up in the same visit. Most pediatric forearm fractures are treated in the ER and never need hospital admission.Sports Collision with Brief Memory LossA high school athlete takes a hard hit during a game, walks off, and cannot remember the play. The headache starts five minutes later. No vomiting, no weakness, no seizure.This is a concussion until proven otherwise. Come in for evaluation. We complete a neurologic exam, decide on imaging based on the HEADS UP criteria, and provide return-to-play guidance grounded in current concussion protocols. Most patients go home the same day with rest instructions and clear escalation triggers.Chemical Splash at WorkAn employee splashes a degreaser into their eye at work. The eye is burning and tearing immediately.Start rinsing on the spot, at the work eye-wash station if available, for at least 15 to 20 minutes. Then come straight to the ER. We continue irrigation on arrival, check pH, run a fluorescein exam, and connect to an ophthalmologist if the cornea is significantly damaged.Major Fall from HeightSomeone falls from a roof, a tall ladder, or down a flight of stairs and cannot move a limb, or has neck pain, or was briefly unconscious.Call 911. Paramedics will board and collar the patient and route directly to a Level I or II trauma center. This is the case where bypassing a freestanding ER for a designated trauma center saves the most time.Sudden Saddle Numbness with Back PainAn adult develops worsening back pain, then notices numbness in the inner thighs and difficulty starting urination.This is cauda equina syndrome until proven otherwise. Call 911. The workup at the receiving hospital is urgent MRI of the lumbar spine and neurosurgical consultation. Time to decompression is the single biggest factor in whether function recovers.How a Freestanding ER Handles Trauma CasesA freestanding ER in Texas is licensed and equipped to evaluate and stabilize the full range of trauma, with the exception of major polytrauma that needs an operating room or ICU on site. For bone, joint, and most head and eye injuries, the workflow looks like this:Triage at the door, with immediate vital signs and a focused trauma examX-ray, CT, or ultrasound within minutes of the order, read by a 24/7 teleradiology servicePain control, IV access, and tetanus update when appropriateSplinting, simple reduction, suturing, or eye irrigation done in the ERSpecialty consultation by phone with orthopedics, neurosurgery, or ophthalmology when neededDirect transfer to a hospital trauma center or specialty service when the injury exceeds what a freestanding ER can fixThe fastest path to definitive trauma care depends on the injury, not on the size of the building. For a single-system injury, a freestanding ER is often the quickest route to answers, because the scan is ordered, taken, and read on site. For major polytrauma, a designated trauma center is the right destination from the start.For lab and imaging context, our on-site lab testing turns around CBC, chemistry, and coagulation results in under 30 minutes when a fracture or head injury workup needs them.How to Decide in the MomentWhen the moment hits, the framework should be simple.Call 911 if: the person is unconscious, has a seizure, is bleeding heavily, has a possible spinal injury, has signs of severe head trauma (one pupil bigger than the other, repeated vomiting, weakness on one side), has chemical exposure to the face or eyes with severe pain, or has fallen from height.Go to a freestanding ER if: the injury is single-system and the patient is alert and stable. Suspected fracture without deformity. Mild to moderate head injury with HEADS UP red flags. Eye foreign body or simple corneal abrasion. Sprain that needs imaging. Concussion evaluation.Go to a trauma center if: there is major polytrauma, a confirmed open fracture with significant blood loss, a known surgical emergency, or you have been told by your specialist to come straight to a specific facility.Do not go to urgent care if: the injury could be a fracture, a head injury with red flags, or any eye injury beyond a tiny foreign body. Urgent care clinics do not have CT, and many do not have X-ray. The time you lose backtracking to an ER is time you cannot get back.For the broader decision framework, our guide to choosing the right emergency room covers the full picture.Pediatric TraumaChildren are not small adults. Their bones bend before they break, their heads are proportionally larger, and a head injury that would seem mild in an adult can be more concerning in a toddler.For pediatric fractures, head injuries, and eye injuries, a freestanding ER is often a strong first stop because of speed and a quieter environment. We have pediatric-sized equipment, weight-based dosing, and clear protocols for when a child needs Children’s Medical Center Dallas or another pediatric specialty hospital instead.Our parent’s guide to pediatric emergency care near White Rock covers the full set of pediatric red flags. Major pediatric trauma, suspected child abuse, head injuries with neurological signs, and complex orthopedic injuries that may need pediatric orthopedic surgery are stabilized with us and transferred fast.Frequently Asked QuestionsHow do I know if it is a sprain or a fracture without an X-ray?You usually cannot. The Ottawa rules give clinical clues, such as inability to bear weight and bone tenderness over specific landmarks, but the only way to be certain is an X-ray. If pain is severe, swelling is rapid, the limb looks deformed, or weight bearing is impossible, treat it as a fracture until imaging proves otherwise.Can I put weight on a possibly broken foot or ankle?If you cannot take four steps right after the injury, the chance of a fracture is high enough to warrant an X-ray. Even if you can, persistent pain over a bone (not just soft tissue) deserves evaluation.When does a head injury need a CT scan?Any head injury with loss of consciousness, vomiting more than once, severe or worsening headache, confusion, slurred speech, seizure, weakness, or drainage from nose or ears needs a CT. Older adults, people on blood thinners, and very young children also have a lower threshold.What should I do for an eye splash before getting to the ER?Start rinsing immediately with cool tap water for at least 15 to 20 minutes. Do not delay the rinse to drive. The duration of irrigation matters more than the speed of arrival.Can a freestanding ER set a broken bone?Yes. We do simple reductions, splinting, and casting in the ER. Complex fractures that need surgical fixation are stabilized and referred to an orthopedic surgeon, often same-day.What if my child fell but seems fine?Watch for the HEADS UP red flags in the next 24 to 48 hours. Any vomiting, drowsiness, behavior change, balance problem, or repeated headache deserves an ER visit. The most dangerous head injuries can hide for hours before they declare themselves.Will my insurance cover an ER visit for an injury?Yes. ER visits are covered under your plan’s emergency room cost-sharing tier regardless of which ER you visit. Texas SB 1264 plus the federal No Surprises Act blocks balance billing for most emergency services.How fast can I get imaging at a freestanding ER?On-site X-ray and CT typically image patients within 20 minutes of the order. Radiologist reads come back through 24/7 teleradiology, often within the next 30 minutes.Where We Are and How to Reach UsER of White Rock is at 10705 Northwest Highway, Dallas, TX 75238, minutes from White Rock Lake, Lakewood, Lake Highlands, Casa View, Casa Linda, and Forest Hills. We are open 24 hours a day, every day, including holidays.If the injury is severe or you suspect a spinal or major head trauma, call 911 first. If the injury is concerning but the patient is stable, call us at (469) 943-2939 and an ER nurse can help triage by phone. For directions and hours, visit our contact page.Knowing the red flags before you need them is the best preparation. Save this page. Save our number. And teach the HEADS UP signs to anyone in your household who has children or plays contact sports.Latest Insights: What to Tell the ER Team: A Medication and Symptom Note Read More ... text: Sprain or Fracture? How to Tell and When to Visit Our ER Near White Rock ER of White Rock Trauma and Injury Medically reviewed by the ER of White Rock Nursing Team |Updated: August 19, 2026 Table of Contents Accidents do not announce themselves. A fall during a weekend hike, a slip on a wet floor, or a sports collision can leave you in a heap of pain in seconds. In those first minutes, one question is almost always the same: “Is this just a sprain, or did I actually break something?”Knowing the difference between the two not only buys peace of mind, it also prevents long-term complications. Some minor injuries do fine at home with ice and rest. Others need imaging and a clinician who can splint, reduce, or refer.If you are weighing fracture treatment near White Rock, knowing when to wait and when to come in is the first step toward a clean recovery. For the broader bone, joint, and trauma picture, our bone, joint, and trauma emergencies guide covers head injuries, concussion, eye injuries, and back-pain red flags too.The Difference: Fractures vs. Severe SprainsTo an untrained eye, a fracture (the medical term for a broken bone) and a sprain can look the same. Both cause pain, swelling, and trouble moving the joint. But they involve completely different structures.What Happens During a SprainA sprain is an injury to a ligament. Ligaments are the tough, fibrous tissues that connect bone to bone across a joint. When a joint twists or stretches past its normal range, the ligaments can be pulled too far or torn outright.You may hear a pop during a sprain. But the bone itself stays intact.The Common Types of FracturesThe American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons (AAOS) defines a fracture as a break that happens when more force is applied to a bone than it can absorb. Clinicians sort them by pattern to plan treatment:Stress fractures: hairline cracks, usually from repetitive overuse rather than a single impact.Greenstick fractures: common in children, where the bone bends and cracks on one side but does not break all the way through.Comminuted fractures: the bone breaks into three or more pieces.Open (compound) fractures: the most serious type, where the broken bone breaks through the skin.Key Signs You Need Immediate Medical CareIf you are not sure how serious the injury is, watch for these warning signs. Any one of them is a reason to come in.Visible Deformity or Exposed BoneThis is the most obvious sign of a fracture. If a limb looks twisted, sits at an unnatural angle, or you can see bone through broken skin, treat it as a medical emergency.According to the National Institutes of Health, an open fracture carries a high risk of deep bone infection (osteomyelitis) and requires urgent surgical cleaning and IV antibiotics.Severe Swelling, Bruising, and Inability to Bear WeightSprains cause swelling, but a fracture often produces deep bruising and near-instant swelling. The biggest tell is weight-bearing: if you cannot put weight on the affected foot or leg without severe pain, or the bone feels unstable, a fracture is much more likely than a sprain.Numbness or TinglingWhen a bone breaks, the jagged edges or the swelling that follows can press on nearby nerves. The National Institute of Neurological Disorders and Stroke notes that numbness, pins-and-needles, or cold sensations in fingers or toes downstream of an injury are signs that blood flow or nerve function may be compromised. That needs urgent evaluation before lasting damage sets in.First Aid: What to Do on the Way to the ERIf you suspect a break, the goal between injury and arrival is to prevent further damage.RICE and ImmobilizationThe NIH-indexed RICE protocol is the standard for acute musculoskeletal injuries: Rest, Ice, Compression, and Elevation. If a bone is clearly out of position, do not try to straighten it.Immobilize: use a splint (a rolled magazine or a board works) to keep the joint above and below the injury from moving.Ice: apply a cold pack wrapped in a cloth for 20 minutes to reduce swelling.Stop bleeding: if the skin is broken, apply gentle pressure with a clean cloth.Why Choose a Freestanding ER Over Urgent Care for a Bone InjuryUrgent care clinics are excellent for sore throats or minor cuts. They often lack the diagnostic tools and specialized staff needed for complex bone injuries.The Value of On-Site X-ray and CTPer the FDA medical X-ray overview, most fractures need imaging to confirm. Our on-site X-ray and CT suite gives our physicians an immediate view of the bone alignment and any soft-tissue damage. At an urgent care, you may be sent elsewhere for imaging, losing valuable time and incurring an extra co-pay.Advanced Pain Management and ReductionA fracture is severely painful. ER teams are equipped with the medications and conscious-sedation options that urgent care clinics cannot offer. If a bone needs to be set back into alignment (reduction), our team can keep you comfortable through the process.What to Expect During Your ER VisitWhen you arrive, stabilization comes first.Initial triage: a nurse quickly assesses pain levels and vital signs.Imaging: you are taken to our X-ray suite within minutes.Physical examination: an experienced emergency physician checks nerve function, circulation, and joint stability.Treatment: depending on the fracture, this may involve a custom splint, a cast, or referral to an orthopedic surgeon for complex breaks.Follow-up: we provide clear discharge instructions and orthopedic referrals to make sure the bone heals correctly.Our fracture treatment pathway walks through the standard workup in more detail.Fast, Compassionate Fracture Care Near White Rock LakeYou should not have to wait hours in a crowded hospital waiting room when you are in pain. Our team at ER of White Rock combines hospital-level technical expertise with the speed and personal feel of a neighborhood clinic.Visit ER of White Rock now for fast relief and expert care.Need immediate care? Call us now at (469) 943-2939.Stay informed with seasonal health tips, first-aid advice, and practical ways to maintain your well-being year-round. Follow ER of White Rock on Facebook and Instagram for valuable health updates.Frequently Asked QuestionsHow can I tell if a bone is broken without an X-ray?Symptoms like visible deformity, a crunching sound (crepitus), and inability to bear weight are strong indicators. But an X-ray is the only definitive way to diagnose a fracture and gauge its severity.Is a fracture worse than a break?No. In medical terms, “fracture” and “break” mean the same thing. The type of fracture (a hairline crack vs. a complete break) determines the severity, not the word used.Can I walk on a broken foot?Sometimes, yes. Stress fractures and breaks in smaller bones can let you walk with manageable pain. That does not mean you should. Continuing to load a broken bone can make the injury worse and delay healing.How long does it take a broken bone to heal?Most fractures heal in 6 to 8 weeks. Recovery time varies with age, the bone involved, and your overall health. Children heal faster; older adults and people with diabetes or smokers heal more slowly.Should I go to the ER for a finger or toe injury?If the digit is bent, numb, the nail bed is crushed, or there is significant swelling, yes. Finger and toe injuries that do not heal correctly can lead to chronic arthritis and loss of motion.What about a hand or wrist injury after a fall?Falls onto an outstretched hand commonly cause wrist fractures (Colles fractures). If there is swelling around the wrist, pain on movement, or any deformity, come in for an X-ray. A missed wrist fracture can leave a permanent deformity.Latest Insights: What to Tell the ER Team: A Medication and Symptom Note Read More ... text: Time Is Brain: Recognizing Stroke Symptoms with the F.A.S.T. Method ER of White Rock Heart and Stroke Medically reviewed by the ER of White Rock Nursing Team |Updated: July 22, 2026 Table of Contents When someone is having a stroke, every second narrows the window for treatment. You have probably heard the phrase “time is brain.” It is not just a slogan. It is a clinical reality.The National Institutes of Health document that roughly 1.9 million neurons die every minute that blood flow to the brain stays blocked. That is the math that turns minutes into permanent disability.If you are anywhere in the White Rock Lake area or East Dallas, knowing the warning signs and where to find emergency stroke care near White Rock Lake can be the difference between full recovery and permanent disability.This guide explains what a stroke actually is, how to recognize one in seconds, and why acting fast is the most important decision your family will make. For the broader cardiovascular emergency picture, our cardiovascular emergencies guide covers heart attack, stroke, and blood clots together.What Happens During a Stroke: Ischemic vs. HemorrhagicA stroke is essentially a “brain attack.” It happens when something blocks blood flow to part of the brain, or when a blood vessel in the brain ruptures. The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) identify two main types:Ischemic stroke: the most common type, accounting for roughly 87 percent of all stroke cases. A clot blocks an artery that supplies oxygen-rich blood to a section of the brain.Hemorrhagic stroke: a blood vessel in the brain leaks or ruptures. The leaked blood puts pressure on nearby brain cells and damages them. High blood pressure and aneurysms are common causes.Either way, the result is the same: brain cells start to die because they cannot get the oxygen and nutrients they need to survive. The two stroke types look similar from the outside but require opposite treatments, which is why a CT scan in the first hour is so important.The Golden Hour of Stroke CareIn emergency medicine, the first 60 minutes after stroke symptoms begin is called the “golden hour.” Treatment can still help after that, but the National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute emphasizes that earlier treatment means more brain function preserved and fewer long-term complications.Reaching an ER inside that window opens the door to advanced imaging and clot-busting medications that simply are not options once too much time has passed.The F.A.S.T. Method for Spotting a StrokeYou do not need a medical degree to recognize a stroke. The CDC teaches the F.A.S.T. acronym as the simplest way to remember the sudden symptoms of stroke.F: Face DroopingAsk the person to smile. Does one side of their face droop or feel numb? An uneven smile is a major warning sign.A: Arm WeaknessAsk them to raise both arms. Does one arm drift downward? Weakness or numbness, especially on one side of the body, is a classic stroke symptom.S: Speech DifficultyAsk them to repeat a simple sentence like “the sky is blue.” Are the words slurred? Are they unable to speak, or hard to understand?T: Time to Call 911If the person shows any of these signs, even if the signs fade, call 911 right now. Write down the exact time symptoms started. That information is critical for the team providing emergency stroke care near White Rock Lake.Atypical Stroke Symptoms You Should KnowF.A.S.T. covers the most common signs, but strokes can sometimes show up in less obvious ways, particularly in women and older patients.Sudden Dizziness, Balance Loss, and Vision ChangesThe CDC notes that sudden trouble walking, dizziness, loss of balance, or coordination problems may signal a stroke affecting the cerebellum. Sudden blurred vision or loss of vision in one or both eyes should never be ignored either.Warning Signs of a TIA (Mini-Stroke)A transient ischemic attack (TIA) is commonly called a “mini-stroke.” According to the National Institute of Neurological Disorders and Stroke, a TIA is caused by a temporary interruption of blood flow to the brain.The symptoms may only last a few minutes and then disappear, but a TIA is a serious warning that a full stroke could be imminent. Treat any TIA as a medical emergency.Why You Should Go to the ER ImmediatelyYou may be tempted to wait and see if the symptoms get better, or to drive yourself to a clinic. Please do not. Calling 911 is critical because paramedics can start stroke protocols the moment they arrive.They can also alert the hospital stroke team so the emergency response is already in motion before you walk through the door.The Narrow Window for Clot-Busting Drugs (tPA)For ischemic strokes, doctors can use a medication called tissue plasminogen activator (tPA). The drug dissolves the clot and restores blood flow.However, NIH guidelines show that tPA generally needs to be given within 3 to 4.5 hours of symptom onset for it to be effective and safe. Wait too long and this life-saving option may no longer be available. Endovascular thrombectomy is approved out to 24 hours in selected patients based on imaging that shows salvageable brain tissue.Rapid Diagnosis and Emergency Stroke Care in East DallasThe Dallas-Fort Worth area is home to some of the country’s leading stroke centers. When you arrive at our ER for emergency stroke care in East Dallas, the team moves at remarkable speed.The standard diagnostic steps include:CT scan or MRI: to determine the stroke type and location.Carotid ultrasound: to check blood flow in the neck arteries.Blood tests: to check clotting speed and glucose levels.Our on-site CT and imaging suite can complete the head scan within minutes of arrival. Our in-house clinical lab turns labs around in under 30 minutes. Our stroke evaluation pathway stabilizes the patient and arranges immediate transfer to a primary or comprehensive stroke center with the right tPA and thrombectomy resources.For the broader question of which ER to choose, our freestanding ER vs hospital ER guide covers the decision tree.Don’t Wait. Get the Stroke Care You Need Today.A stroke can change a life in minutes. If you or someone in front of you shows any F.A.S.T. sign, do not hesitate. Call 911 immediately. ER of White Rock offers around-the-clock stroke evaluation with minimal wait times and specialized diagnostics.Visit ER of White Rock now for fast relief and expert care.Need immediate care? Call us now at (469) 943-2939.Stay informed with seasonal health tips, first-aid advice, and practical ways to maintain your well-being year-round. Follow ER of White Rock on Facebook and Instagram for valuable health updates.Frequently Asked QuestionsCan a stroke happen at any age?Yes. While the risk goes up with age, strokes can happen to anyone, including children and young adults. Lifestyle factors and underlying medical conditions play a significant role.What is the difference between a stroke and a heart attack?A heart attack is a circulation problem in the heart, while a stroke is a circulation or bleeding problem in the brain. Both are life-threatening emergencies.Should I take aspirin if I think I am having a stroke?No. Do not take aspirin unless a doctor tells you to. If the stroke is hemorrhagic (bleeding), aspirin can make the bleeding worse.Why is calling 911 better than driving to the ER?Emergency Medical Services (EMS) can start treatment immediately and are trained to bypass hospitals that are not equipped for stroke care, taking you directly to a facility equipped for emergency stroke care near White Rock Lake.Are stroke symptoms different in women?Sometimes. Women may have unique symptoms such as sudden hiccups, nausea, or generalized weakness in addition to the traditional F.A.S.T. signs.Latest Insights: What to Tell the ER Team: A Medication and Symptom Note Read More ...
